items.headline: ULA delays Vulcan rocket launch carrying 40 Amazon broadband satellites
items.title: ULA delays Vulcan rocket launch of 40 Leo satellites for Amazon
items.scifi_hook: A massive rocket with six boosters is set to loft a fleet of internet satellites after a brief postponement.
items.eli5: The launch was pushed to tomorrow; the Vulcan rocket will put 40 Amazon low‑Earth‑orbit satellites into space.
items.why: Delays affect Amazon's plan to expand global broadband coverage.
items.text: A United Launch Alliance Vulcan, equipped with six solid rocket boosters, stands ready for launch at Cape Canaveral’s pad 41. The rocket will carry 40 Amazon Leo satellites to orbit. Image: Michael Cain/Spaceflight Now. Update 9:45 a.m. ET: ULA has scrubbed today’s launch attempt and rescheduled for tomorrow at 12:32:30 p.m. EST (1732:30 UTC). United Launch Alliance is set to return its Vulcan rocket to flight Friday, nine months after a solid rocket booster malfunction prompted the U.S. government to pause its use of the 215-foot-tall, non-reusable rocket. The upcoming mission, Amazon Leo LV-01, serves a private customer, Amazon, which tasked ULA with carrying 40 broadband internet satellites to expand its Leo constellation — the first of 38 Vulcan launches Amazon purchased. Liftoff from Space Launch Complex 41 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station is scheduled for 12:54 p.m. EST (1754 UTC), at the opening of a 29-minute window. The rocket will fly on a northeasterly trajectory upon leaving the pad. Spaceflight Now will have live coverage beginning 30 minutes prior to liftoff. Space Force weather forecasters predict a 90 percent chance of acceptable weather, with scattered high clouds and northwest winds of 15 to 20 knots. After two burns of the Vulcan’s Centaur upper stage, the satellites will begin separating about 70 minutes after liftoff, roughly 285 miles up, in 16 separation events over about 25 minutes, according to a ULA mission diagram. items.headline: Canadian firms advance lunar rover designs for upcoming Moon base
items.title: Canadian Lunar Rovers Ready for Next Phase—And An Earlier Launch
items.scifi_hook: Three Canadian companies are building two‑ton rovers that could drive on the Moon within a few years.
items.eli5: Canada is funding companies to design smaller, faster lunar rovers for future Moon missions.
items.why: Supports NASA's Artemis lunar base plans and builds domestic space capability.
items.text: Three Canadian companies are racing Moon-cart concepts. Canadensys, MDA Space, and Mission Control collectively received C$14.6M ($10.3M) in July 2025 for a Phase 0 lunar-utility-rover study supporting Artemis. And now, work is almost done. Phase shift: This year, NASA unveiled its plan to build a Moon Base —an undertaking that will require a transportation network that includes big rovers. As a result, CSA is expected to boost funding for its rover projects, and a new RFP should drop within days that will downselect to two companies to keep building in 2027 alongside science-instrument procurements. MDA Space is a competitor in the rover procurement, as well as the maker of Canadarm3—originally intended to be used for Gateway. A company official told Payload that lunar mobility will enhance Moon Base support alongside possibly repurposed robotics, under examination through a funded task authorization with CSA. Moon Meccano: CSA is asking industry to design a fully robotic rover, roughly the size of two pickup trucks side by side, that must fit on a 1.5m-by-1m pallet. Mid-design phase, CSA chose to shelve designs for the four-ton rover initially envisioned for 2034—at least temporarily—and asked companies to instead target a two-ton product that could ship ~3 to ~4 years faster. items.headline: Microscopic solar panels aid alignment in 3D‑printed tissues
items.title: Microscopic solar panels could help shape 3D-printed biological tissue
items.scifi_hook: Tiny solar cells power bioprinting without bulky wires, letting cells grow like a living circuit.
items.eli5: Small solar panels give electricity to printed tissue, keeping cells correctly oriented without big wires.
items.why: It could make lab‑grown organs cheaper and more reliable.
items.text: Bioprinting uses living cells and molecular signals to produce biological tissues and even whole organs, building them layer by layer in the lab. To keep the bioink, or blend of cells and materials that power this printing, correctly aligned to grow a target tissue, researchers use electricity. However, this typically requires bulky electronic interfaces and invasive wiring.

items.headline: New study argues economics, not trucks, will solve space junk
items.title: Solving the space junk crisis isn't just about counting trash—it's about control and economics
items.scifi_hook: A NASA scientist proposes market‑driven control methods instead of giant space garbage trucks.
items.eli5: Cleaning space debris will rely on clever pricing and control, not just scooping it up.
items.why: Effective debris removal protects satellites and future space missions.
items.text: If people ever think about cleaning up space debris, they typically think of something equivalent to a giant garbage truck in the sky, collecting lost astronaut tools and dead satellites, then hauling them back down to Earth to be deposited in a landfill. But dealing with space debris doesn't work that way, and a new paper by Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, available as a preprint on arXiv, makes a good argument as to why. We typically cover Turyshev for his work on the solar gravitational lens idea.
